text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) usually has no symptoms, which is why it is widely known as the "silent killer".

Most people with high blood pressure feel completely normal and do not realize their pressure is high. You cannot typically feel the condition, meaning it can cause silent damage to your heart, brain, and kidneys over many years without any warnings.
You can learn more about the condition and its underlying factors through the Mayo Clinic.
When blood pressure is moderately or subtly elevated, some people may occasionally notice non-specific signs, though these are not definitive:

list.snippet: Pounding sensation in the ears, neck, or chest

text_blocks.snippet: Extremely high blood pressure (a reading above 180/120 mm Hg) can trigger a dangerous spike known as a hypertensive crisis or emergency, which requires immediate medical care. If your blood pressure is above 180/120 mm Hg and you experience any of these severe symptoms, call 911 immediately:

list.snippet: Shortness of breath or difficulty breathing
Sudden, severe headache unlike any before
Signs of a stroke, such as numbness, weakness on one side of the body, facial drooping, or trouble speaking

text_blocks.snippet: For more guidance on critical readings, visit the American Heart Association.
If you'd like, let me know:

list.snippet: Your recent blood pressure readings if you have them
Whether you are experiencing any specific symptoms right now

perspectives.author: heart_transplant_doc
perspectives.title: High blood pressure rarely gives a warning sign. That’s why it’s called the silent killer. Most people wait until symptoms appear, but the damage can begin long before you feel anything. Your blood vessels stiffen. Your heart works harder. Your kidneys and brain can slowly take the hit. The biggest problem often isn’t awareness. It’s delay. “I’ll watch it.” “It’s not that bad yet.” “I’ll deal with it later.” But later can become years. The good news? Earlier action changes outcomes. Checking your blood pressure, improving sleep, moving more, reducing ultra-processed foods, managing stress, and getting the right treatment at the right time can protect your heart before a crisis happens. Don’t wait until your body forces you to care. Save this for yourself. Share it with someone you love. Your future heart will thank you. Educational only — talk with your doctor about your personal blood pressure goals and treatment plan.
